Back in '83 or so, I laid out a circuit board to allow a ZIF socket
to come out of the top of a Videocade cartridge and since there were
tracks running between IC pads I had it professionally etched. Also
included a way to invert the top two address lines to allow mixing
2K, 4K and 8K games on the same 2764 EPROM using a quad 7486 X-OR
and two dip switches. Not until I read Ward Shrake's description of
his MultiCart using plain old OR gates did I realize that it would
be enough to switch, say, the upper 4K down to the bottom half; the
lower 4K didn't really need to swap to the upper half at that time!
Oh, well, I think the price for the TTL chips was about the same...

Anyway, I only made these for friends - usually giving them a Bally
machine at the same time, since I only knew of one bought from JS&A
(though the motherboard was ruined by an incontinent Irish Setter).

"
Here's what you have. You have an almost untouched Bally / Astrocade unit
except for 3 things:

1) The shielding was removed, which was a common fix to prevent the large
chip inder the keypad's wiring (Commonly called the "Custom Data" chip} from
overheating. The shielding was originallt there to keep RF from the unit to
effect nearby televisions. This was quite a problem when the unit was
originally designed abd the TVs had tube-type tuners. With the advent of
digital tuning used in ALL newer sets, this isn't an issue.

2) There appears to be a larger than normal heat sink on that chip. This is
a GOOD thing.

3) The small notch in the back near hand control 3 jack has been removed.

This was so that the 300 baud interface could be used with the original
BASIC (One with a GOLD label and NO jack or LED).

The long whir wire is there because when they originally designed the PCB,
the filter (Largest of the 2 silver cylinders in that area) was too far away
fron the power supply, so they needed to get it electrically closer.

I hope this answer some of your questions.

5037:
I am going to give you a description of the "mysterious and highly complex" 300-baud format:

The basic element is the "bit". One bits are stored as 8 short pulses, and 0 bits as 4 long pulses. This way, both 1 and 0 bits have the same length.

The tape recording starts with a "strobe" signal consisting of some 256 one bits. I am not sure of the exact bit count for this, but I am quite sure the exact value is irrelevant, as the signal seems to not be reliable until some time after it starts, and the 300-2000 baud file converter doesn't seems to take it in account.

Well, we have this long "header", then just a sequence of bytes straight from the character table, and that's all!

Bytes are encoded this way: They always start with a zero bit. Do you remember the strobe signal I mentioned? Well it is a sequence of 1 bits, then, the sequence is interrupted by a 0 bit. Then, it is followed by eight bits, consisting the character data itself, recorded from the most significant bit to the least significant bit. And then, there are recorded one bits, for an unspecified time (i am not sure of the precise count, but the converting utility doesn't take it into account). after this, a zero bit, eight data bits, n 1 bits, and so on.

And, at the end of the file, a $FF byte is recorded in the same way described above.

The keyboards recieved were DEFINATELY NOT the ZGRASS, from any part
of the development!

One is a JAMECO 610 for use with a UART (that did not come with this
unit) which enabled it to run bit serial into the 300 baud interface
so as to allow keyboard entry with BB or EB.

SDS SYSTEM MONITOR (with overlay)
COLOR BASIC
FAWN DUNGEON (unfinished with assembly notes)
(one demo program that I can't remember the name of that appears to
be a forunner of "256 color display" from the AB handbook)
TWO system roms (WHITE?)

and a whole box full of custon chips!!! (DATA, ADDRESS, and IO)

The ROMS (other than the 2 system ROMS) were in 2716's and
the "DUBBLE BUBBA" that came with these chips won't fit into my
arcade! It seems that the arcade Bill L. bought recently may not be
totally unique.

Upon using my own "ROM reader" I discovered that I may not have 
copied a couple of EPROMS that Richard Degler lent me properly. These
2716's wanted the program line high (address line A11 in a 2732) in
order to read at all! I probabaly didn't do it that way when I copied
the two 2716's that Richard sent. Sorry!

Mike W.

5132:
dZ80 and others assume all of a binary is machine code and
happily disassemble data and text strings without allowing
you to mark them as data or text strings, so a lot is wrong.

IDA free is supposed to scan for reachable code and mark the
rest as data bytes, then allow you to (I)nteractivly (D)is-
(A)ssemble from there.  Unfortunately, even though it claims
to work on Z-80 code even as freeware, it only allows 80x86
to be selected as the source unless you pay the license fee.


So is there a good Z-80 dis-assembler around? I had to use a
hex editor and an old copy of the source code for LIFE (with
a lot of changes made since printing it out) to debug MESS.


The problem was inside a macro SETOUT system call, where the
screen interrupt mode was set to turn an interrupt back off
if the CPU didn't handle it right away, like when interrupts
are disabled until a certain screen scanline used for timing
is being waited for. But MESS didn't generate an interrupt!

If the screen interrupt mode was cleared an interrupt would
remain on until the CPU acknowledged it, then MESS _would_
generate interrupts, just not timed to the screen scanline.


Not sure if that was clearer than the MESS BugZilla report,
but anyway, the latest version (named LIFEMESS.BIN on here)
has the EI/HLT timing restored but still might not work on
an actual Astrocade. The real fix would be to make the way
that the numbers are erased the same way that old cells are
cleared (it's done at the same time!) but that would take...

a decent Z-80 disassembler!!

Not true.  DZ80 allows you to tell which areas to disassemble, it just takes
several steps before you get much of the program done.  Here is what
you need to do:

1)  When dz80 starts, click the Options button.
2)  Under Disassembly Control, in the Start and End fields, type in the
    addresses that you want disassembled.  Everything else will just be
    defined as bytes.

As you learn more about the disassembled program, disassemble more
of the program using this method.  It's not fast, but it works-- and it is MUCH
faster than using a hex editor.

I noticed that the website for dz80 is down.  I searched for the program online.
While I DID find it, I didn't find even the version that I have online at
Ballyalley.com (only older versions).

As alternatives to dz80, you might check into what disassembler is used
over in the Gameboy, Spectrum or Colecovision programming circles.

program?  It used to be that you had to compile your own version of MESS
with the debugger built-in if you wanted to use it, but that is no longer the

Anyway, I have at least gotten back on track with tape archiving.  I
glanced through all the tapes (and there are a lot), and while most
are Arcadian submissions, and some aren't even labeled, there are also
some commercial programs mixed in.  I'm particularly interested in
these since we often don't have them available as either recordings of
source code scans, making them completely lost.  So, I pulled out some
of the more interesting tapes, concentrating on 2000 baud at the
moment, and have so far gotten 15 working programs, helping to fill in
a few more gaps in the archive.  There is nowhere near a complete
collection of commercial programs here, but I do hope to get a lot
more taken care of.  Expect many in the future to be 300 baud, though.
 Here's what I got.

Six programs by Fred Rodney--Project Cyclops Radar Base, Astro
Analyst, Rhythm Box In 3-4 Time, Rhythm Box in 4-4 Time, Morse Code
Trainer, and Morse Code II.  Unfortunately, I haven't been able to get
Memomax working, which would complete the collection of Fred Rodney's
commercial programs.  Project Cyclops Radar Base has some good
animation, but the gameplay didn't excite me.  Astro Analyst is along
the same lines as WaveMaker's Character Analysis, but with more shapes
and less detailed personality descriptions.  I don't really get into
these, but maybe it's just because it said I was vain and intolerant.

there are programs to generate a musical beat and to teach Morse code.

Three programs by Tiny Arcade--two copies of Star Siege (Revised) and
Quadron.  The Star Siege tape actually was labeled as revised, and is
a slight improvement over the version now on-line.  It has different
sound and you can start a new game by pulling the trigger rather than
hitting a key.  The two copies aren't byte-for-byte identical, but I
couldn't tell a difference.  Quadron seems to play the same as the
version now on-line, but doesn't have even a simple title screen.
These are good games.  I need to check out some more Tiny Arcade
stuff.  There's at least a bit more in with the tapes I got.

Two programs by John Collins--Treasures Of Cathy and Checkers (III).
These two programs are an example of something only mentioned as a
brief text ad in the Arcadian.  Of known programs, ones like this are
probably the least likely to be archived, so I'm glad to get a few.
Treasures Of Cathy seems like a fairly complex dungeon-crawler type
game.  I didn't get very far, though.  If anyone can figure out how to
get through the door, let me know.  Checkers (III) attempts to make a
complete checkers game with AI.  It's buggy, though.  I suppose the
previous two versions were even more buggy.

One program by Steve Walters--Pepsi TV Game.  This programs doesn't
seem to be referenced anywhere.  Maybe it's an Arcadian submission
that wasn't printed.  It seems to be a tool for keeping track of
bottle cap numbers for a contest Pepsi was running.  You can even save
your data to tape.  Of course, this isn't particularly useful 26 years
later.

Three programs by New Image--Guess Five, Quickdraw, and Skunk.  We
already have versions of Quickdraw and Skunk which have better title
screens.  Guess Five, however, was previously unarchived.  It's a
Mastermind-type game.  So, this fills in a hole for one of the more
important tape software companies.

These were and are consoles and computers from the same time period.  Many people on this group collect computers and consoles from the classic era.  Often, postings about other machines bring normally silent folks out of the woodwork and they make a posting, sometimes their very first one.

These conversations are always a big circle-- it always gets back to the Astrocade.  For example, I never would have mentioned that I had only heard of the Z-Grass first in a book that I read in about 1994.  There was so much disinformation about the Astrocade-- and still is-- that when I hear about other orphaned systems with no support I always feel a bit of sympathy for them.

When I first became really interested in the Astrocade in about 1999, about twenty or so carts were dumped.  Not bad for such an unknown system.  Just talking about the console a bit on rec.games.video.classic in late 2000 got me connected with Ward Shrake (I met him in March 2001).  In a short time (on the first day that I met Ward!) all of my carts had been dumped (even the carts that had already been dumped-- Ward dumped them again just to compare them to previously dumped carts).  Suddenly there were far more dumped carts.  Soon, I got in touch with Mike White.  Then Ward contacted Mike.  Then there were even MORE dumped carts.  With just a handful of people talking on the phone, writing letters and using email we were able to make a substantial dent into what was archived.  Sure, Ward did the archiving (thanks, Ward!), but it was other folks that brought all of these ROMs and carts to him so that he could do it.  Eventually Glenn Saunders suggested that I start a forum, and this message board was formed.  Then, Bob Colbert wrote Ballybin and Astrowav, which lead to the archival of the tapes.  I archived some tapes, but then lost interest-- it is hard and tedious work.  Paul Thacker came along a few years later and, working with tapes compiled by Mike White, really became the prime mover behind tape archiving.

My first ambition for Ballyalley.com was to just get the Arcadian newsletters archived.  Then a few other items got added to the list.  With the message board and with contact with other Arcadian folks more items made their way to the website.  Look at Ballyalley.com now.  It's LOADED with information about the Astrocade!  This never would have happened without the first few steps that were taken when people listened to me on rec.games.video.classic and made some suggestions.  If others had closed their eyes and ears to such an unknown system when I brought it up, the Astrocade would be even LESS known today (if such a thing is even imaginable!).

So, while I'm not for talking about other systems ALL of the time here (especially VERY well-covered systems like Atari or Intellivision), in this instance, I like the topic.  It IS related to the Astrocade, if for no other reason than its obscure nature-- but really, isn’t there more to it than that?  The APF has an official computer expansion, the one promised upgrade that just never could make it out the door from either Bally or Astrovision, Inc.  The APF had a newsletter that kept users going after the machine was discontinued.  The APF had very few cartridges, just like the Astrocade.  The APF had BASIC.  The APF had homegrown talent that created and shared tape games.  The two machines have more in COMMON between them than differences.

Wheh!  I guess what I’m trying to say is that I don’t mind listening and talking about a system that isn’t talked about anyplace else.

Bill Loguidice, on Fri 2/08/08 at 8:27 AM, wrote:
>>
You probably don't recall all the details, but the Astrocade that I picked up with the cartridge that accepted EPROM's, would that be something that I could use to [make or test EPROMS].

Well, sure.  I'm not sure what size of EPROM that the cartridge you have accepts.  If it accepts 8K EPROMs (the biggest that the Astrocade can use), then you're in good shape.  If it uses 4K EPROMs, or less, then it STILL can be used but it would be somewhat limited.

>>
I realize I would need an EPROM burner and the right EPROMs, but I was wondering if everything else was there that I would already need?
>>

Let's just presume that the cart accepts 8K EPROMs, here is what else you would need (some of which you have already mentioned):

1) EPROM Programmer - If you only want to burn EPROMs, then a modern programmer for a PC will work fine.  They range from cheap (under $100) that have limitations, to burners that cost a grand (that can do anything but wash your dishes).  My Pocket Programmer cost about $250.  Check out ebay-- you can often find deals on there.  If you plan to read older cartridges (for archiving, for instance), then you would be better off with an older programmers or one of the VERY expensive models.  Ward swears by his Promenade C1 programmer for his C64.  Another option is to build your own if you're electronically inclined (plans for simple 27xx EPROM burners are pretty common on the Internet).

2) EPROM Eraser - An EPROM needs to be erased before it can be used.  This requires ultraviolet light, supplied by an EPROM Eraser.  You can get these pretty cheaply (say, fifty dollars or less).

3) Circuit Board for EPROM - Since EPROMs have different pin assignments, you cant just desolder a ROM from a cartridge's circuit board and then use it.  In your case, you already have a cartridge usable for an EPROM for the Astrocade (a great first step!).  In other classic gaming you can just go to atariage.com and order pre-made circuit boards for the 2600/5200/8-bit and Colecovision (I find this AMAZING!).  There is probably a place to get the boards for Vectrex too, but I dont know where.  As for the Intellivision, it uses some odd scheme and Im not sure how that would work.  Most of the time, when all else fails, you can get a cart and hack it up to work.  Sometimes this is nearly impossible, for instance in the case of the Timex Sinclair 2068, because even the original cartridges are nearly impossible to find.

4) EPROMS  Of course you will need the actual EPROMs to program.  Youll need one of the following.

2716 2K EPROM
2732 4K EPROM
2764 8K EPROM
27128 32K EPROM.

Atariage.com sells EPROMs for $3 each.  EPROMs have always been given to me.  Anyone else care to mention some other suppliers?

5) Electronic Components  You may also need some resistors, inverters, capacitors or miscellaneous gates.  What youll need all depends on what cartridge and system youre working with.

>> 
I've ALWAYS wanted to get into making my own cartridges [...] but found the whole idea rather unapproachable
>>

If youre not going to hack-up a cartridge then youll just need to be able to solder, know which is pin 1 on a chip and thats about it.  It gets more complicated when you want to hack-up a cartridge.

Good luck... and ask any other questions that you need!  Oh, and sorry it took so long to answer this question.  For whatever reason this posting was seen as spam by Yahoo and I just approved it.  Sorry about that.

mentioned in the DNA manual will generate an interrupt even in the
borders to the left and right of the screen while the "regular" one
won't.  I never saw a game that used a light pen, so these both should
be turned off - that's why I wondered what code those examples used was
snipped from.

I had (have?) a little circuit board that hung on the light pen
connector with a 555 timer and a potentiometer that you could adjust to
bring the system to a crawl handling all the interrupts.  This worked
for Basic, where you could write a 5 to that port, and then watch it
print a character.  Instead of drawing it left-to-right and
top-to-bottom it does it backwards!
